## Overview

The shared groundwork for ENG-14843: let each journey say which seed it needs, and let a check read saved database rows as well as screen text. We're doing this so new areas such as the AI SDR and campaigns can be added without special cases in the runner, and so checks can prove what a feature saved, not only what it showed.

## Problem

The runner only knows the `crm` seed, so every new seeded journey needs another special case (Ebubeker's review point on ENG-14784). Checks can only assert text on the page. The Preview Seed workflow hard-codes its scenario list (`crm|flag`) in two places.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[bun verify run journey] --> B[Today: runner special-cases crm]
  A --> C[NEW: journey declares seed scenario and marker]
  C --> D[Runner seeds from the declaration]
  D --> E[Browser steps]
  D --> F[NEW: database check steps, fixture workspace only]
  E --> G[Evidence]
  F --> G
```

## What's included

* The journey definition names its seed scenario and marker contract, and the runner reads it.
* A read-only database check step, scoped to the fixture workspace.
* The Preview Seed workflow takes its allowed scenarios from one list in code.

Also from Ebubeker's QA on ENG-14784 (6 Oct 2026):

* On a preview, `open` without a seed screenshots the signed-in workspace, which is a production copy, so screenshots and the contact sheet can show customer names and emails. Default preview runs to the seeded `verify-fixture-pr<N>` workspace, or block when the target isn't a fixture workspace.
* When `.env` sets `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `gh` gets a 404, `doctor` reports "could not read PR" instead of naming the token. Retry with gh's own login on 404 too, or name the token in the error.

## Done when

- [ ] Adding a seeded journey needs no change to the runner.
- [ ] A journey can fail on a saved row as well as on page text, and a check can't read outside its fixture workspace.
- [ ] Adding a scenario updates the workflow's allowed list from one place.
- [ ] A preview run never saves screenshots of a production-copy workspace.
- [ ] A bad `GITHUB_TOKEN` is named as the cause, not the PR.

## Implementation context

Code at 3f1c1bd, the head of Acquisity/Acquisity#6891:

* Runner: `scripts/verify/cli.ts` (`journeySeed`, `seedLocal`).
* Journey shape and steps: `scripts/verify/journey.ts`.
* Scenarios: `scripts/verify/scenarios.ts`.
* Preview seed result: `scripts/verify/preview-seed.ts`.
* Workflow list: `.github/workflows/preview-seed.yml` and its check at L77.
* Tests: `apps/web/tests/scripts/verify/`.

The plan is in the suggested implementation comment. Audits: `~/Documents/CRM/verify-everything-2026-10-07/audits/`.

relatedSnapshot.title: Master: Let a smart view list the people who opted out of texts or are do not contact
relatedSnapshot.description:
## Overview

A rep cannot build a smart view of the people who replied "stop" to a text, and there is no list of people who opted out of texts or are marked do not contact. The product already detects a texted STOP and stops texting that person, but nothing surfaces them, so a missed opt-out reply goes unnoticed and the person stays contactable by call and email.

## Problem

An opt-out reply can arrive and be missed. Marking someone do not contact is a manual step on the person record, and no view lists the people who opted out of texts or carry the do-not-contact flag, so a rep cannot work a queue of them. The rep asked for exactly that list, because missing one reply is a compliance risk, not just a preference.

## Root cause

The saved-view field registries declare every key a view may filter on, and none of them covers a message's content, text consent, or do-not-contact state, so the filter editor and the AI filter builder have no field to run the condition on.

* `apps/web/lib/crm/view-field-keys.ts` (`BUILT_IN_FIELD_KEYS`, `CONTACT_VIEW_FIELD_KEYS`): the allowed key set, and saves refuse keys it does not list. The contact keys cover identity, tags, owner, call-history rollups, appointments, payments, communication counts, activity, last-touch facts and thread lifecycle.
* `apps/web/lib/crm/filter-field-registry.ts` and `apps/web/lib/crm/derived-filter-field-registry.ts`: the field contracts the editor menu and the AI prompt are generated from.
* `apps/web/components/crm/crm-data-table/field-configs/build.ts` (`buildFieldConfigs`): throws when a configured field has no registry entry, so the editor cannot offer a field the registries do not declare. The "Latest communication" column exists but is marked `filterable: false`.
* `apps/web/lib/crm/scope-prompts/shared-guidance.ts` (`buildUnsupportedSection`): the AI builder refuses a condition it cannot express rather than approximating it.

Detection is not the gap. `isTextOptOut` in `apps/web/lib/crm/sequences/auto-reply.ts` matches a whole message of stop, stopall, unsubscribe, cancel, end, quit, optout or opt out, and `apps/web/lib/services/inbound-sms-processor.ts` applies it through `applyInboundSmsConsent` in `apps/web/lib/services/sms-consent-service.ts`, which records the opt-out and blocks further texts. Do-not-contact is derived from a status option carrying the `do_not_contact` flag or from the workspace phone list (`apps/web/lib/crm/contact-contactability.ts`), and set by hand through `apps/web/lib/crm/contact-dnc.ts`.

## Blast radius

1,256 organizations and 1,907 users, counted 2026-10-13 on the production read replica.

* `SELECT count(DISTINCT organization_id) AS orgs, count(*) AS rows FROM crm_sms_consent WHERE status = 'opted_out'` returned 1,256 organizations and 15,805 rows; 12,325 of those rows are tied to a person record.
* 885 of those organizations also hold at least one live saved CRM view (the same opt-out set joined against `crm_view` where `deleted_at IS NULL`).
* 1,907 distinct active members (`member.deleted_at IS NULL`) sit in those 1,256 organizations.

Only 11 organizations have any received text stored in `crm_message`, so the native CRM text surface is live in a few workspaces while the opt-out record itself is widespread.

## Proposed fix

Add a view field that answers whether a person replied an opt-out keyword, or more simply whether they are opted out of texts or do not contact, and let it be filtered and saved from both the filter editor and the AI builder. The answer is derivable from records that already exist (the text-consent status, the status option flag, the workspace phone list), so it can ship as a filter on its own, without any message-content search.

## What's included

* In scope: one filterable field (or a small set: opted out of texts, do not contact) wired through the registry, the editor config, the SQL compiler and the sample-mode twin, with the parity suites updated.
* Excluded: searching message bodies for an arbitrary word. The earlier smart-view master parked that as the largest piece of work, and the fixed opt-out keywords do not need it.
* Related and owned elsewhere: the in-app do-not-contact phone list in CRM settings, and the parked message-content search from the smart-view master.

## Regression seam

Boundary: the saved-view filter path through `crm.view.list` and the filter editor, compiled by `compileFilterGroups` in `apps/web/lib/crm/advanced-query-builder.ts` and mirrored in sample mode. Trigger: a saved view whose only rule is the new field. Red before: the editor does not offer the field, and a hand-built rule on its key is refused or matches nothing. Green after: the editor offers it and the view lists exactly the people who opted out of texts, and no one else. A parity suite in `apps/web/tests/lib/crm/` proves the registry, the editor config and the compiler agree.

## Done when

* A rep can add the new field in the People filter editor and in the AI filter builder, save the view, and reopen it with the rule intact.
* The saved view lists exactly the people who opted out of texts, or who carry the do-not-contact flag, as the field is defined, and no one else.
* The parity suites cover the new key: registry, editor config, AI prompt and compiler agree, and sample mode mirrors the server compiler.
* A regression test at the named seam proves the red-before, green-after behaviour.

## Reports

* ENG-15266 Smart views not blocking the word "stop"

relatedSnapshot.title: Build power dialler session start, pause, resume, and queue building
relatedSnapshot.description:
> **Context.** Glossary: master ticket ENG-12173. For THIS ticket: a power dialler "**session**" = one calling run: a rep pressed Call on a saved view, and the system works through that list. This ticket builds the backend lifecycle: start a session, build its queue from the view, pause, resume, end. "**Materialization**" = copying the view's matching rows into the session's own queue table, done in chunks of ~500 so a 10,000-row list starts Company One (think paginated import, with a stored **cursor** = a bookmark recording how far we've read). "**Controller token**" = a secret that marks WHICH browser tab is allowed to drive the session, so a second tab can't fight the first. Deal views need one extra rule: a deal is a sale, not a person, so we resolve each deal to the actual person to phone (primary linked contact with a phone, else the first linked contact with a phone). Why it matters: this is the spine of the power dialler; the claim/dial logic (next ticket) hangs off the sessions and queues you build here.

**Size:** M/L · **Design:** none · **Blocked by:** ENG-12177
**How it should work (Close reference):** starting a session from a saved list (GIF): <url>

### Overview

An SDR opens a saved contact or deal view and starts power dialling. The server creates their session and builds the calling queue from the view, in the view's order. The rep can pause, resume, or end the run, and can only have one run at a time. Starting again while a run exists gives a choice: pick the old one back up, or start fresh.

### Problem

ENG-12177 gives us the tables but nothing fills them. There is no way to start a session, build the queue from a view, keep the queue topped up for big lists, pause or resume, or stop a rep from running two sessions at once.

### Solution

Build the server-side session lifecycle and queue building. The queue is built from the view in chunks (materialization: copying matching rows from the view into the session's queue), so huge lists start fast and still run to completion. No cap on list size.

Technical notes:

* `dialer.startSession` accepts a contact view or a deal view.
* Deal rows resolve to one person by ONE deterministic rule, acceptance-tested: the deal's primary linked contact IF that contact has a phone; otherwise the first linked contact by creation order that has a phone. That contact's primary number is dialled (locked decision: primary number only in v1). Deals with no linked contact holding a phone get no item (items require `contactId`) and are counted in the phoneless count, never silently dropped.
* Queue building runs server-side through the query-builder internals, NOT paged `getContacts` (its 100-row page cap and permission truncation make it unsafe for queues). Chunked with the stored `materializationCursor` (last sort key plus id tie-breaker for deterministic order). First chunk ~500 rows. Top-up runs inside `claimNext` (the claim-protocol ticket) when pending items drop below ~25.
* Per-session single writer: a session-row lock (`FOR UPDATE`) fences top-up, the 5-minute cron sync, and `syncNow` so they never overlap.
* Session state machine, server-enforced, idempotent transitions: active | paused (reason: user, view_deleted, or access_lost) | completed | abandoned. Completed and abandoned are terminal. An idle worker sweeps BOTH active and paused sessions whose `lastActivityAt` is older than 2 hours straight to abandoned and releases their leases, but never while a live call is bound to the session. Idle expiry is never shown as a pause.
* `lastActivityAt` is refreshed by `claimNext`, `completeItem`, `skipItem`, pause, resume, and heartbeat.
* Starting a session on ANY view while one exists prompts end-or-resume. "Start From Scratch" (and starting on another view) is ONE transaction: mark the old session completed, release the old session's non-live leases in that same transaction, create the fresh session. This satisfies the one-session database rule with no gap. The swap is REFUSED with a clear error while a live call is bound to the old session: end the call first.
* Counts are tracked as separate numbers, not one blended figure:
  * source rows in the view,
  * unique dialable contacts after duplicate collapse (two deals or rows sharing one person become one queue item): this is the primary progress denominator the panel shows,
  * duplicate-collapsed count (how many source rows merged into an existing person),
  * phoneless count (rows with nobody to dial),
  * a cursor-exhausted flag (true once the whole view has been read into the queue).
* Controller fencing lives HERE, not in the later UX ticket. `startSession` and `resumeSession` issue and rotate the `controllerToken` and `controllerGeneration`. Every rep-initiated dialler mutation validates the token server-side from day one. System writers (the sync cron, Twilio callbacks) are trusted paths and never carry the token. The wrap-up/recovery ticket later adds only the takeover UX.
* Permission matrix, gated per action, never as one bundle:
  * Dialling: `FEATURES.POWER_DIALER` feature flag composed with the `voice.make_call` permission.
  * Editing or overriding a call outcome: `manage_call_events` (claim-protocol ticket).
  * Unknown-number quick-create: contact-create rights; without them the flow degrades gracefully (call logs unlinked, no create prompt).
  * Server-side on every mutation: organization membership, session ownership, and saved-view access at start.
  * Verify the intended SDR role holds the full set (`voice.make_call` + `manage_call_events` + contact-create) and document the degraded behavior for each missing capability.

### Scope

* In: `startSession`, pause, resume, end, heartbeat; queue materialization with cursor and top-up trigger contract; session state machine and idle sweep; the deal-to-contact rule; the five count grains; controller token issuance, rotation, and validation; per-action permission gating.
* Out of scope: claiming and completing items (claim-protocol ticket), view sync and the Continue vs Start From Scratch skip rules (queue-sync ticket), all UI, takeover UX.

### Acceptance criteria

 1. When a rep starts a session from a contact view, then a session row and the first ~500 queue items exist in the view's sort order, and the counts and cursor-exhausted flag are correct.
 2. When a rep starts a session from a deal view, then each deal resolves by the rule: primary linked contact if it has a phone, else the first linked contact by creation order with a phone; the chosen contact's primary number is stored; a deal with no linked contact holding a phone creates no item and increments the phoneless count.
 3. When two deals in the view share one contact, then exactly one item exists for that contact, `sourceEntityIds` holds both deals, and the duplicate-collapsed count reflects the merge. Unique dialable contacts is reported as the progress denominator.
 4. When the view has more matches than one chunk, then top-up (triggered from `claimNext` when pending < ~25) continues under the session lock until the cursor is exhausted, with stable order across chunk boundaries, no duplicate items, and no stranded matches.
 5. When a rep with an active or paused session starts a session on any view, then they are prompted to end or resume; if they choose Start From Scratch, then in one transaction the old session becomes completed, its non-live leases are released, and the new session is created.
 6. When a live call is bound to the current session, then Start From Scratch and any cross-view start are refused server-side with a clear error, and nothing changes.
 7. When a session's `lastActivityAt` is older than 2 hours, then the idle worker moves it (active or paused) to abandoned and releases its leases; when a live call is bound, then the sweep skips that session.
 8. When `claimNext`, `completeItem`, `skipItem`, pause, resume, or heartbeat run, then `lastActivityAt` is refreshed.
 9. When a rep-initiated mutation arrives with a stale controller token or generation, then the server rejects it; when `startSession` or `resumeSession` runs, then a fresh token and generation are issued.
10. When the feature flag is off or the caller lacks `voice.make_call`, then every session procedure rejects server-side; when a session, view, or item id from another organization is passed, then the mutation is rejected.
11. When a rep lacks contact-create rights, then unknown-number handling degrades as specified: the call still logs, unlinked, and no create prompt is shown.
12. When the same transition is replayed (duplicate pause, duplicate resume), then the state does not corrupt (idempotent transitions).

### Design (Name 1)

Backend ticket — for reference, the UI this drives: 27 · power dialer preflight (session start, queue counts) and 28 · power dialer active — bottom bar (running session). Full screen map on master ENG-12173.

relatedSnapshot.title: Keep notification sync working for people with more than 2,000 Name 7 items in one list
relatedSnapshot.description:
## Overview

When someone has moved to the new notification feed, we still keep their Name 7 items in step with what they do. To find the matching Name 7 item, we read at most 2,000 items in each of their Name 7 lists (open, snoozed, Done, Done and snoozed). Anyone with more than that gets stuck, so this needs fixing before anyone is switched.

## Problem

Finding one Name 7 item stops after 2,000 items in a list and gives up with `inbox_scan_truncated`. Two places use it:

* the job that copies a person's read, Done and snooze changes back to Name 7, which then blocks that change for good;
* the switch check's stable read of one Name 7 item, which then fails.

ENG-14780 removed the backfill report group that used to flag these people when they had overdue reminders (Acquisity/Acquisity#6890). So the report no longer warns about them, and the 5 October run showed at least 2 people over the limit. People without overdue reminders were never flagged.

## Proposed fix

Find a Name 7 item by reading each list page by page with a cursor until the end, the same way the history import now does, instead of stopping at 2,000 items. Use the same matching rules the import uses, so the two can't drift apart.

## What's included

* Removing the 2,000-per-list stop from finding a single Name 7 item, for both callers above.
* A call limit per lookup or per run, so one very large inbox can't use up the sync job's Name 7 calls.
* Excludes: the switch itself (ENG-13839 step D), the backfill and history import, and the Name 7 call budget's size.

## How it should work

* A person with any number of Name 7 items gets their read, Done and snooze changes copied to the right Name 7 item.
* A missing item, two items for the same delivery, a changing listing or a failed call still stops safely with the same reasons as today.
* Hitting the call limit stops safely and is retried or reported. It never picks a wrong item.

## Who can do what

Not applicable: an internal sync job with no new access.

## What the user sees

Nothing directly. People with large Name 7 inboxes who switch to the new feed keep their read, Done and snooze state in step instead of being stuck.

## Done when

* A test with more than 2,000 items in one list finds the right item and copies the change.
* Duplicate, missing and changing-listing cases still fail with the same reasons.
* A test proves the call limit stops a very large inbox safely.
* Finding a single item and the history import share one set of matching rules.

## Open questions

What call limit should one lookup or one sync run have? Recommended: reuse the per-person 1,024-call budget for each lookup, and leave the item pending to retry when it runs out.

## Expected outcome

No Name 7 inbox size can stop a switched person's notification state from staying in step, so step D can switch anyone the backfill clears.

## Implementation context

AI context.md holds the code paths, evidence and suggested approach as of 6 October 2026.
